About: Relative Velocity in One Dimension

Source

Topic
Kinematics · Relative motion in 1D (NCERT Class 11)
Concept
Changing frames subtracts the frame's velocity from every velocity — nothing physical changes.
Serves
Galilean transformation of velocity; sign conventions in 1D; the antisymmetry vBA = −vAB.
Inquiry
Predict what a passenger on A sees B doing when both travel the same way at 20 and 28 m/s.
Misconception
"Relative speed is the sum of the speeds." It is the sum only when directions oppose; same direction gives the difference.

Relative Velocity in 1D
Two trains on parallel tracks · Ground frame

Guided Inquiry

1 · The set-up

Two trains run on parallel tracks. Right now the sliders are set to vA = 20 m/s and vB = 28 m/s — both moving to the right, in the ground frame. The trackside poles are anchored to the ground.

The simulation is already playing — watch from the ground for a few moments (pause with ⏸ any time). Then go on.

2 · Predict

A passenger sits on train A. B is 8 m/s faster than A in the ground frame. What does A's passenger see B doing?

3 · Switch to A's frame

Click A in the Observer frame selector below. Watch what happens: train A stops dead in the centre, and the trackside poles begin to stream past. That streaming is the ground moving at −vA in A's frame.

The readout now says v of B relative to A. You should see about +8 m/s — exactly the prediction.

4 · Flip B negative

Now drag vB down to about −28 m/s. B is now barrelling to the LEFT while A still moves right. In A's frame, B closes on A at vB − vA = −28 − 20 = −48 m/s.

This is when the two speeds really do add — because they point in opposite directions and the signs do the bookkeeping for you.

5 · What actually changed

Nothing physical. Switching frames just subtracts the frame's velocity from every velocity. Same direction → the numbers subtract to a small relative speed. Opposite directions → they subtract to a large one. The equation vrel = vB − vA handles both cases without a special rule.

Explore freely. Try vA = vB = 25 m/s — B sits frozen alongside. Try any pair and toggle the frame; A's arrow collapses to a dot in A's frame, B's collapses in B's.

01

At a glance

Two trains run on parallel tracks past a row of poles fixed to the ground. You can watch from the ground or ride along on either train, and compare what each observer sees the other train doing.

What you'll learn

  • How the velocity of one train reads when you measure it from the ground, from the other train, or from itself.
  • Why the sign of a velocity matters whenever two motions are compared.
  • How to find the velocity of one body relative to another in one dimension.
Two trains over a row of ground poles. Each arrow is a train's velocity as the ground measures it.

What's on screen

  • Train A on the upper track and Train B on the lower one, each with a velocity arrow and a value in m/s.
  • Poles along the ground with distance labels in metres.
  • Observer label at the right: whose point of view the scene is drawn from. A dashed YOU box marks the train you ride.
  • Readouts panel: the other train's velocity in that view, and the relative speed.
See itWatch from the ground with vA = +20 m/s and vB = +28 m/s. Watch for: both trains moving right past the fixed poles, each arrow carrying its own value.

03

A moving observer subtracts their own velocity from every velocity

A velocity is always measured by someone. An observer who moves at velocity u reads every velocity v as

v′ = v − u
Positive means to the right for every observer.

A passenger on Train A has u = vA. Train A's own velocity becomes vA − vA = 0, so it stops dead in the view. Train B reads v′B = vB − vA, the velocity of B relative to A. The poles are at rest on the ground, so they read 0 − vA = −vA and stream backward.

With vA = +20 m/s and vB = +28 m/s, A's passenger sees B at 28 − 20 = +8 m/s and the poles at −20 m/s.

See itSwitch the observer frame to Train A. Watch for: Train A at rest in the centre, B's arrow reading v′B = +8 m/s, and the poles streaming left.
04

Opposite directions give the largest relative velocity

Let B head left, vB = −28 m/s, while A still heads right at +20 m/s. In A's view v′B = −28 − 20 = −48 m/s. The speeds 28 and 20 add here because the velocities point opposite ways. For the same direction the same rule gives 28 − 20 = 8, the difference.

So one rule covers both cases, with the signs included:

vBA = vB − vA
The relative speed is |vB − vA|.

At −48 m/s the 400 m gap closes in 400 / 48 ≈ 8.3 s, and the sim's note says so. The panel below uses the sim's own sliders.

vA vB

These sliders move the sim too.

See itRide Train A, then set vB = −28 m/s. Watch for: B's arrow pointing left and reading v′B = −48 m/s, with B sweeping across to A in about 8 s.
05

Swapping the two observers reverses the sign

Now ride Train B, so u = vB. Train A reads v′A = vA − vB, which is exactly the negative of what A's passenger reads for B:

vAB = −vBA
Each train sees the other moving the opposite way.

With the opening values, B's passenger sees A at 20 − 28 = −8 m/s, and the poles at −28 m/s. A drifts backward in B's view while B creeps forward in A's. Both describe the same fact: the gap between the trains grows by 8 m every second.

The size is the same for both observers, so the relative speed has no favourite observer.

See itSwitch the observer frame to Train B. Watch for: Train B at rest in the centre and A's arrow pointing left, reading v′A = −8 m/s.
06

Equal velocities freeze the other train in view

Set vA = vB = 25 m/s. Then vB − vA = 0. From A's seat B hangs motionless 400 m ahead, and its arrow shrinks to a dot. The gap never changes.

The relative speed is the rate at which the gap changes. When A is behind B and faster, the gap closes at vA − vB and A draws level after

t = 400 m / (vA − vB)
Valid only while vA is greater than vB.

With vA = +30 m/s and vB = +10 m/s, that is 400 / 20 = 20 s. If vA is less than or equal to vB, the gap never closes.

See itRide Train A with both velocities at +25 m/s. Watch for: B's arrow collapsing to a dot reading v′B = 0 m/s, and B staying put ahead of A.
07

Where it matters

  • Overtaking. A car at 90 km/h (25 m/s) passes a truck at 72 km/h (20 m/s). The car gains on the truck at only 5 m/s, so a pass takes a long stretch of road.
  • Head-on approach. Two cars at 60 km/h each, heading toward each other, close at 120 km/h. The severity of a collision depends on this relative speed, not on either car's speed alone.
  • Boats and rivers. A boat that moves at 5 m/s relative to the water, in a river flowing at 3 m/s, moves at 8 m/s relative to the bank downstream and 2 m/s upstream. The same signed rule applies, with the water as the moving frame.
  • Choosing a frame. Many problems become simple from the viewpoint of one body, because that body's own velocity drops out.
08

Summary

In one line. A velocity is always measured by some observer, and changing the observer changes the value you read for the same body.

Key points

  • An observer moving at velocity u reads every velocity as v′ = v − u.
  • The velocity of B relative to A is vBA = vB − vA, and vAB = −vBA.
  • The relative speed |vB − vA| is the sum of the speeds for opposite directions and the difference for the same direction.

Common mix-ups

  • "Relative speed is the sum of the two speeds." That holds only when the velocities point opposite ways. In the same direction it is the difference, and the signed rule vB − vA handles both.
  • "If A sees B at +8 m/s, B sees A at +8 m/s." B sees A at −8 m/s. Swapping the observer flips the sign.
  • "Riding on a train changes what actually happens." It changes only the readings. The trains meet at the same instant in every frame, 8.3 s for vA = +20 and vB = −28 m/s.

Things to try on your own

  • With vA = +30 m/s and vB = +10 m/s, predict when A reaches B, then run it and compare with the sim's note.
  • Set vA = +10 m/s and find the vB that makes B read −30 m/s in A's view.
  • Choose any pair of velocities, ride each train in turn, and check that the two relative velocities are opposite.
